result.summary: Hercules sacks Elis but spares Pisa because of a Delphic oracle, and gives Elis to Phyleus. The text then traces the Elean kings down to Eleus and tells how the one-eyed mule's driver Oxylus became guide of the Dorians and was promised Elis.

scenes.title: Hercules conquers Elis, spares Pisa
scenes.summary: Hercules sacks Elis and punishes Pylos but is stopped from attacking Pisa by an oracle. He yields Elis to Phyleus, and the Elean women pray to Athene for children.
scenes.stakes: Pisa faces destruction by Hercules' army; Elis has lost its young men.

scenes.title: Kings of Elis after Augeas
scenes.summary: Augeas dies and his son and the sons of Actor share the kingdom. Homer's catalogue and the descent to Eleus are used as evidence.

scenes.title: Oxylus guides the Dorians
scenes.summary: An oracle tells the Dorians to take a three-eyed leader; they choose Oxylus, the muleteer with a one-eyed mule. He advises sea travel and is promised Elis; his exile from Aetolia is explained.
scenes.stakes: The Dorians need a way back to the Peloponnese; Oxylus was exiled for killing his brother.

notable_quotes.reason: The Delphic oracle that saved Pisa from Hercules.

analysis.text: Oracles shape the fate of cities and peoples, often through riddling words fulfilled in odd ways, like the one-eyed mule.
Pausanias reconciles local Elean tradition with Homer's catalogue and the Dorian return to build a coherent royal genealogy.

language_notes.text: Pytho is the old name of Delphi, seat of Apollo's oracle. The speaker is the god, who says he holds Pisa in trust.
Bady is Pausanias' transliteration of a local Elean word meaning 'sweet'; he explains it in the parenthesis.
'In a private capacity' means they never held royal power; Pausanias argues that they, too, ruled, contrary to the idea that only the other three did.
Homer's catalogue is the list of Greek ships and leaders in the Iliad, Book 2, used here as historical evidence.
'Return' refers to the Return of the Heraclidae, the descendants of Hercules reclaiming the Peloponnese with the Dorians.
'Force their way through the isthmus' means attacking overland across the Isthmus of Corinth, the land route into the Peloponnese.
Heraclidæ means the descendants of Hercules, here led by the sons of Aristomachus.

context_notes.text: Phyleus was Augeas' son, who had sided with Hercules against his father and was exiled to Dulichium.
Athene is the goddess of wisdom and war; here she is also invoked for childbirth, as 'Mother'.
Naupactus and Molycrium are on the north shore of the Gulf of Corinth; sailing from there avoided the isthmus.
Quoit throwing was a discus-like athletic contest; accidental killing normally required exile for purification in Greek custom.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias adds his own judgment, reading the oracle as the reason Pisa survived.
The parenthetical 'I fancy' shows the author speculating openly about naming customs, marking his guess as such.
The riddling oracle is solved by a chance, humble sight: a muleteer with a one-eyed mule makes three eyes.
